how-many-wholesale-bunches-do-you-need-f.text:
← back to the calculator

How many wholesale bunches do you need for a wedding?

A recipe is written in stems: 85 garden roses, 60 spray roses, 40 ranunculus. A wholesale invoice is written in bunches, and a bunch is a fixed count you buy whole or not at all. Getting from one to the other means rounding, and rounding the wrong way — or at the wrong point in the calculation — either under-orders the job or quietly pads the quote. Here is the arithmetic, worked on a real five-variety recipe.

Round the shrink allowance in first, then round the bunches up

Two roundings happen, in this order and not the other way round. First, add a shrink allowance — breakage, blown blooms, processing loss — to the stem count the recipe calls for, and round that up to a whole stem. Second, divide by the bunch size and round up to a whole bunch. Doing the bunch rounding first and adding shrink to the result buys a fraction of a bunch, and no wholesaler sells one.

Worked on 85 stems of a ten-stem variety with an 8% shrink allowance: 85 × 1.08 = 91.8, rounded up to 92 stems needed. 92 ÷ 10 = 9.2, rounded up to 10 bunches. The invoice is for 100 stems against a recipe that called for 85 — not because the shrink allowance is generous, but because the tenth bunch was always going to be bought in full once the count passed 90.

The same arithmetic across a full recipe

Applied to every line of a five-variety wedding recipe, with an 8% shrink allowance and ten-stem bunches throughout:

LineStems neededWith 8% shrinkBunches orderedStems purchasedLeftover
Focal (garden rose)85921010015
Secondary (spray rose)606577010
Texture (ranunculus)404455010
Greenery (eucalyptus)303344010
Accent (stock)25273305
Total240——29050

Five lines, five separate roundings — the leftover on each line depends on where that line's own stem count happens to fall against its own bunch size, not on the size of the wedding. A recipe that lands just past a boundary on every line rounds up every time; one that lands just under rounds up on none of them. Both are normal, and neither is a sign anything was priced wrong.

Where the leftover stems actually go

Fifty stems left over on a 240-stem recipe is not fifty stems of waste — it is stems that were always going to be part of the bunches the wholesaler sells, whether the base recipe used them or not. The ordinary destinations, roughly in the order studios reach for them:

  • Boutonnieres and corsages. These use a handful of stems each and are easy to forget to budget for separately — the leftover from the main recipe often covers them without a dedicated line.
  • Extra bud vases for a welcome table, escort-card table, or restroom counter — small, cheap arrangements that use up odd numbers of stems well.
  • Topping up an arrangement that looks thinner after transport than it did in the shop, which is common enough that having spare stems on hand is worth more than the stems themselves.
  • A take-home bouquet for the couple, or a thank-you arrangement, if none of the above use up what is left.

Whatever is left after that is a reasonable thing to compost or donate. None of this needs to be quoted to the client in advance — the bunch rounding already priced the stems, so what becomes of them afterward doesn't change what was charged.

Common questions

Why can't I just order the exact number of stems the recipe calls for?

Because a wholesaler doesn't sell single stems of most varieties — they sell bunches, and a bunch is a fixed count you either buy whole or don't buy at all. A recipe calling for 85 garden roses from a variety that ships ten to a bunch means the invoice is for 90 or 100, never 85. There is no line item for five-ninths of a bunch.

How do you work out how many bunches to order for one line of a recipe?

Add the shrink allowance to the stem count first, then divide by the bunch size and round up. For 85 stems with an 8% shrink allowance, that's 85 x 1.08 = 91.8, rounded up to 92 stems needed, divided by a bunch size of 10 and rounded up again to 10 bunches — 100 stems purchased. Rounding at the end instead of the start of that sequence gives a different, wrong, answer on some lines.

What should I do with the leftover stems?

They are not waste unless you treat them that way. The usual destinations are boutonnieres and corsages (which use a handful of stems each and are easy to under-budget for separately), extra bud vases for a welcome or gift table, topping up an arrangement that looks thin after transport, or a take-home bouquet for the couple. Whatever isn't used is a reasonable thing to compost or donate rather than something to feel you must price a use for in advance.

Does raising the shrink allowance always add another bunch?

No — only when it pushes the stem count across a bunch-size boundary. On a line already sitting well under a full bunch's worth of headroom, a one- or two-point change in the shrink percentage does nothing to the bunch count, because the rounded-up total doesn't change. On a line sitting just under a boundary, the same change adds a whole bunch. That is why the effect of shrink is a per-line question, not a flat percentage of the total.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely on your own device; nothing you enter is uploaded.

Open the wedding florist proposal calculator → — it runs this same per-line rounding on your own recipe and reports the bunch count, the leftover, and the resulting gross margin.

No warranty. This page is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. It is not purchasing, business, or financial advice and does not replace your own wholesaler's order minimums or your own judgment about a specific recipe. Bunch sizes and availability vary by grower, season, and supplier — verify both against your own wholesale account before you order.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

Private by default

Everything on this page runs in your browser. Your wholesale costs, markup, and client figures are never uploaded, there is no account, and nothing is saved when you close the tab. Copy shareable link is the one way these figures leave this device, and only because you choose to send them: they ride in the page's URL fragment, which a browser never puts in a request line or a Referer header. Common questions

Why does buying in bunches change the price so much?

Because a recipe is written in stems and a wholesaler sells bunches. A recipe calling for 85 garden roses from a variety that ships in tens means you buy 100 and pay for 100 — the other 15 are yours whether the design uses them or not. Multiply that across six varieties and the difference between the recipe's stem count and the invoice is real money. A per-stem markup never recovers it, because the markup was applied to a cost you never actually paid. This calculator buys whole bunches on every line and reports the gap as its own figure.

Should the shrink allowance be a percentage on the flower cost?

No, and it is wrong in both directions. Adding the percentage to the line's cost at the end buys a fraction of a bunch, which no wholesaler sells. On 100 stems of a ten-stem variety the allowance genuinely needs a whole eleventh bunch, and a 5% cost bump does not pay for it — you arrive short. On 95 stems the allowance already fits inside the ten bunches the recipe forced, and the same 5% pads the quote for a bunch nobody buys. This calculator adds shrink to the stem count first and rounds bunches afterwards, so the allowance is always something you can actually purchase.

Is labour really a third of the flower total?

It is a reasonable rule for a bouquets-and-centrepieces wedding, where the hours track the stems. It breaks on installations. An arch, a hanging piece, or a late strike takes hours and comparatively few stems, so a percentage of flowers under-prices exactly the events that cost you the most time. This calculator prices design and on-site labour by the hour and shows what the percentage rule would have quoted beside it, so the gap is a number you can look at. The rule never changes the total — it is reported for comparison only.

Why is the studio's own design time counted as revenue but not as a cost?

Because it is billed, not paid out. The gross profit line subtracts the cash that actually leaves the studio for this event — flowers at purchase cost, hard goods, and anything paid to freelance designers or install crew. Your own hours are what the proposal is charging for, so counting them again as a cost would show every event you work yourself as less profitable than the identical event you hired out. If you want to see your own time as a cost, put it in the freelance crew payout field.

Does anything about my costs or my clients get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only, there is no account, and nothing you type is uploaded. Nothing leaves this device unless you choose to send it: the Copy shareable link button puts the figures on the form into the page's URL fragment, which a browser never sends to a server or into a Referer header, so it reaches only the person you hand the link to. Your wholesale prices and markup are commercially sensitive, so note that anyone who has that link can read the numbers in it — send it the way you would send the numbers themselves. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-a-recipe-markup-spreadsheet.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. a recipe markup spreadsheet

Nearly every wedding florist prices from a spreadsheet: list the recipe, multiply the stems by a per-stem price, apply a markup, add a labour percentage. It is quick, it encodes recipes nobody else has, and for a studio whose events are similar in shape it works. The two answers separate at one specific point — the sheet prices stems, and a wholesaler sells bunches — and this page is about where that matters and where it does not.

What each one is for

A recipe markup spreadsheet is the right tool for holding your recipes and turning them into a number fast. It is the accumulated knowledge of your studio, and no calculator replaces it. What it does not do on its own is convert a stem count into a purchase — because a purchase happens in whole bunches, and a spreadsheet cell does not know a variety's bunch size unless you make it.

This calculator takes the same recipe and buys it: it adds the shrink allowance to the stem count, rounds each line up to whole bunches, marks up what was actually bought, prices design and on-site labour by the hour, and reports the gross margin. It also reports what the per-stem basis would have quoted, so the difference between the two methods is a figure rather than an argument.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What is in this design, and how many stems?Your spreadsheet. That is what it is for, and this calculator takes the answer as input.
What will the wholesale invoice actually say?This calculator — it rounds each line to whole bunches instead of pricing loose stems.
How much does the shrink allowance really cost?This calculator — the allowance enters the stem count before the bunch rounding, so it is always a purchasable quantity.
What should I charge for a wedding like the last one?Either one — if the shape is similar and your sheet is tuned, the sheet is faster.
Is this install-heavy event priced for the hours it takes?This calculator's hourly labour lines, next to the percentage rule for comparison.
Is the margin on this proposal where I want it?This calculator — it subtracts only the cash that leaves the studio and reports the margin against your target.

The one number that separates them

Take a recipe line calling for 85 garden roses from a variety that ships in bunches of ten, at $38 a bunch. A spreadsheet multiplies 85 by the per-stem price of $3.80 and gets $323. The wholesaler sends nine bunches — ten, once an 8% shrink allowance is added — and invoices $380. The $57 difference is not an error in either method; it is the cost of the stems the design does not use, which somebody pays for either way.

Across a five-variety recipe that difference was $135 on the worked example this calculator opens with. Applied at a 3.5× markup, it is $472.50 of quoted price — because a markup multiplies whatever cost basis it is given, and a stem-count basis is smaller than the invoice. That is the whole of the disagreement, and it is arithmetic rather than opinion.

Nothing here says or implies that a recipe markup spreadsheet is a bad way to price a wedding. It is a different job: a spreadsheet stores and multiplies a recipe, and this calculator converts that recipe into a purchase. Studios that already encode bunch sizes in their sheets are doing the same thing this page describes, and will find the two answers agree.

Common questions

What does a recipe markup spreadsheet do well?

It is fast, it is yours, and it holds the one thing no tool can supply — your actual recipes, built up over seasons of real weddings. For a studio whose events are similar in shape, a sheet that multiplies stems by a markup and adds a labour percentage produces a defensible number in a couple of minutes, and there is nothing wrong with that.

Where does a stem-count spreadsheet and a bunch-based calculator disagree?

On what the flowers cost. A sheet multiplies the recipe's stem count by a per-stem price; a wholesaler sells bunches, so the studio pays for whole bunches whether the design uses them or not. The two agree exactly when every line divides evenly into its bunch size, and they diverge on every line that does not. The markup then multiplies the difference, so a modest gap in cost becomes a larger gap in the quoted price.

Can I just add a percentage to the spreadsheet to cover it?

You can, and many studios do — but a flat percentage is right only by coincidence on any given event, because the rounding waste depends on how each line's stem count sits against its bunch size, not on the size of the event. A recipe that happens to divide evenly gets padded for nothing; one that lands just over a bunch boundary on four lines is still short. A percentage is a guess at a figure that is exactly computable.

Why price labour by the hour rather than as a share of flowers?

Because the share-of-flowers rule assumes hours track stems, which they do on a bouquets-and-centrepieces wedding and do not on an install. An arch or a hanging piece takes hours and comparatively few stems, and a late strike takes hours and no stems at all. Pricing those by the hour and reporting the percentage rule alongside shows the gap instead of hiding it — neither figure is forced on you.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely on your own device; nothing you enter is uploaded.
